data.title: Leopold Aschenbrenner plots 'Situational Awareness 2.0' comeback - report
data.description:
Leopold Aschenbrenner is plotting an reboot for his hedge fund Situational Awareness just four months after the AI-focused vehicle nearly collapsed under leveraged bets and required an emergency rescue from billionaire Ken Griffin's Citadel, according to a media report published Wednesday.

In recent weeks, the 25-year-old has discussed plans for "Situational Awareness 2.0" with prime brokers and investors, including a return to leveraged trading and raising new capital, the Financial Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

The move represents a reversal from July, when Aschenbrenner issued a mea culpa vowing he would no longer borrow money from lenders to amplify his bets. His success hinges on convincing Wall Street he can manage risk after assets plunged from more than $20B to needing an emergency rescue in a matter of days this past summer. The fund still manages more than $10B, mainly in private stakes, the FT reported.

Situational Awareness holds an approximately $5B stake in AI giant Anthropic —where Aschenbrenner's wife serves as chief of staff to CEO Dario Amodei—that is expected to appreciate markedly after the initial public offering.

Aschenbrenner has also discussed raising additional capital from outside investors in the new year, though plans have not been finalized, people involved in the talks said, the FT reported.

Aschenbrenner reportedly has been in discussions with Jefferies to set up a prime brokerage account, following an earlier rejection this year over concerns that the fund wasn't adequately hedged. Meanwhile, Situational Awareness is also partnering with the specialist brokerage Clear Street.

The San Francisco-based hedge fund during the summer had to strike an emergency deal with Citadel to offload most of its public equities at a discount in order to repay lenders like Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan Chase —both of which had provided financing despite Aschenbrenner's minimal trading background. JPMorgan later terminated its lending to the fund. Situational Awareness continues to oversee a modest public portfolio that includes positions in SharonAI and data center developer CleanSpark .

data.title: Canadian dollar hits 19-month low after hawkish Fed governor comments
data.description:
By Fergal Smith

The Canadian dollar weakened to a 19-month low against its US counterpart on Wednesday as recent strength in US economic data and hawkish comments from an influential Federal Reserve policymaker helped underpin the greenback.

The loonie was trading 0.2% lower at 1.4325 per US dollar, or 69.81 US cents, after touching its weakest intraday level since April 2025 at 1.4340.

  • "I think that the US dollar was looking a bit heavy until we had the stronger-than-expected jobs growth numbers and the hotter-than-expected inflation numbers," said Marc Chandler, chief market strategist at Bannockburn Capital Markets. "This has turned the dollar around broadly, not just against the Canadian dollar."

  • The US dollar added to recent gains against a basket of major currencies as Fed Governor Christopher Waller said the central bank needs to become more aggressive in its response to inflation that he fears is changing public psychology about prices.

  • "My work shows a stronger correlation between changes in the greenback and changes in the 2-year yields," Chandler said.

  • The US 2-year yield has moved about 21 basis points further above the Canadian equivalent since the start of the month to a gap of 148.5 basis points.

  • The Bank of Canada could also raise interest rates in December — investors see a roughly 60% chance of a hike. (0#CADIRPR)

  • The BoC's practice of issuing scenarios on inflation and growth keeps the central bank accountable and helps make monetary policy more effective, Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle said.

  • The price of oil, one of Canada's major exports, fell after US crude and fuel inventories data added to expectations of a supply surplus. US crude futures were trading 4.1% lower at $82.50 a barrel, which could ease concerns about the inflation outlook.

  • Canadian bond yields fell across a flatter curve, tracking moves in US Treasuries, with the 10-year (CA10YT=RR) down 2.5 basis points at 3.795%.

data.title: Fox's Roku takeover faces fresh legal challenge from Newsmax
data.description:
Newsmax has sued Fox Corporation in an effort to block its $22 billion acquisition of Roku, arguing that the combination would weaken competition in the rapidly expanding market for free, ad-supported streaming television.

The lawsuit, filed on Wednesday in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, seeks to halt Fox's integration of Roku and reverse the transaction unless Fox agrees to sell either Tubi or The Roku Channel.

Newsmax alleges that the combined company would control more than 70% of the free ad-supported streaming TV market, raising concerns about competition and access to distribution platforms.

Fox announced on November 6 that it had completed the acquisition, ahead of the timeline previously outlined by the companies following months of regulatory scrutiny.

The complaint also challenges commitments Fox made to the US Justice Department, including assurances that non-Fox content would not face discriminatory treatment in search results. Newsmax argues those pledges are unenforceable because they were not incorporated into a consent decree or court order.

Newsmax , which operates Newsmax TV and the Newsmax2 streaming channel, said it depends on The Roku Channel for distribution. It also alleged that Fox had previously declined to carry Newsmax on Tubi.

Additionally, the company owns an attractive mix of strategic investments in development-stage biopharma firms that could also lead to value creation.

Trading at an EV/2027E EBITDA multiple of ~6x, Innoviva shares “are amply reflecting the aforementioned royalty dynamics, with a high-growth hospital business that alone can justify multiple expansion,” Amsellem wrote.

data.title: Global GDP to grow 2.8% in 2027, with corporate earnings growth slowing and stocks rallying – Goldman Sachs
data.description:
Goldman Sachs Research forecasted global GDP will grow 2.8% in 2027, up from 2.7% this year, as declining energy prices and robust artificial intelligence investment outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy.

The economies of the US, Japan, and the UK are among those projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates, according to the investment bank's research division.

The risks to that forecast "are tilted to the downside," said Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research.

Renewed Middle East escalation could spark another energy price surge, large fiscal deficits could push up long-term yields, especially in France, and AI capital expenditures could fall short of expectations due to capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress, or weaker demand, he said.

Japan stands out as an exception, where consumption tax cuts, defense spending, and investment plans are forecast to boost GDP growth by 0.7 percentage point, according to the economist.

AI investment is expected to keep boosting growth, with Goldman analysts forecasting that nominal global AI investment will rise to $1.8T in 2027 from $1.1T this year, mostly driven by an over $500B increase in U.S. hardware spending.

The economists estimated that AI investment will boost GDP growth by 0.4 percentage point globally. Under the firm's baseline forecast for a steady decline in energy prices, inflation should slow in 2027, with Hatzius expecting core PCE inflation to ease from 3.2% at the end of 2026 to 2.4% at the end of 2027.

Stock markets from New York to Tokyo are expected to extend their rally in 2027, even as corporate earnings growth and AI investment slow in most regions, said Peter Oppenheimer, chief global equity strategist in Goldman Sachs Research.

"We expect the equity bull market to continue," Oppenheimer said, though he also anticipated more volatility than in recent years.

In the U.S., corporate earnings growth is expected to slow from 36% to 11%, in part because hyperscaler capital spending is expected to grow more slowly and energy prices are easing, according to the strategist.

The Goldman team highlighted three key investment themes for 2027. Growth stocks , , present opportunities as the price-to-earnings ratio for technology stocks , globally has fallen sharply, now sitting in the 20th percentile of its historical band over the past 20 years, the analysts noted.

Defensive equities could also offer opportunities, with Oppenheimer suggesting a focus on companies that benefit from lower bond yields, such as U.S. firms that consistently buy back their stock, while Europe , stands to gain the most from cheaper energy prices.

data.title: KFC franchisee declares bankruptcy
data.description:
A major franchisee of Yum Brands’ KFC restaurants has filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection, citing declining sales and rising costs.

Tasty Chick’n LLC and its affiliates filed Monday in U.S. Bankruptcy Court for the Southern District of Texas in an effort to prevent the parent company of KFC from terminating its franchise agreement and seizing its KFC and co-branded Taco Bell restaurants. The franchisee currently owes close to $16M in unpaid royalties to Yum owed since November 2025. The company also owes $67.2M to lenders.

Yum notified the franchisee nearly a year ago that it was in default of its franchise agreements.

According to court papers, Tasty Chick’n has closed or will close 72 KFC restaurants co-branded Taco Bells and has requested the court to let it drop all its leases.

Tasty Chick’n is the most recent of major franchisees going bankrupt over the past several months. Bloomin’ Brands’ largest Outback Restaurant franchisee, Out West, filed for bankruptcy protection in November, while Wendy’s has surfaced as the stalking horse bidder for Meritage Hospitality Group’s restaurants.

data.title: Wheat, corn, soybean futures sag as dollar firms
data.description:
Chicago wheat futures fell roughly 4% on Wednesday, giving up gains from the previous session as the dollar hit a 19-month high, making US grains less competitive globally, analysts said.

Corn fell about 2% while soybeans posted more modest declines as lower crude oil added to bearish sentiment.

As of 1:07 p.m. CST (1907 GMT), Chicago Board of Trade December wheat futures were down 25 cents at $5.70-1/4 per bushel, the contract's lowest level since January.

CBOT December corn was down 11 cents at $4.35-3/4 a bushel and January soybeans were down 9-1/2 cents at $12.16 a bushel.

Strength in the dollar pressured the grains complex. The greenback firmed on expectations for an interest rate hike next month.

"The strength in the dollar is definitely into the grain markets," said Tom Fritz, a partner with EFG Group in Chicago.

"There is lots of technical selling involved here. The funds are adding to their wheat shorts. They're adding to their shorts in corn, and I believe they're still liquidating in soybeans," Fritz said.

Managed funds still held a net long position in CBOT soybean futures as of November 10, weekly data from the US Commodity Futures Trading Commission showed.

Traders awaited a meeting between the leaders of the United States, China and Russia for diplomatic developments on Russia's war in Ukraine. US President Donald Trump is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China on Thursday, in addition to the trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, US and Russian officials said.

Wheat had rallied on Tuesday after a Ukrainian attack destroyed the central road section of the Crimea bridge. Debris blocked navigation through the Sea of Azov, threatening further disruption to massive Russian wheat exports.

But with shipping traffic in the Azov-Black Sea zone already heavily reduced for months due to drone attacks and incoming Southern Hemisphere harvests set to bolster global supplies, market reaction was moderate, traders said.

Grain markets are also monitoring developments regarding US-China relations, with Chinese purchases of US agricultural goods a central part of the countries' ongoing trade truce.

data.title: Republican Senator Cornyn blocks Trump judicial nominee in Texas
data.description:
Key points:
  • Cornyn withholds blue slip support for T. Elliot Gaiser
  • White House expects all Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by year's end
  • Trump nominated Gaiser after election for federal judge seat in Dallas

By Nate Raymond and David Morgan

US President Donald Trump's efforts to secure Senate confirmation of as many conservative judges as possible before Democrats take control of the chamber suffered a setback on Wednesday after a Republican senator blocked one of his nominees from advancing.

Outgoing Republican Senator John Cornyn of Texas withheld support for US Department of Justice official T. Elliot Gaiser to appear before the Senate Judiciary Committee for a hearing on Wednesday where it could take up his nomination to be a federal judge in Dallas.

Cornyn's decision not to return a so-called blue slip backing Gaiser marked the latest instance of a Republican senator not supporting a White House-backed judicial nominee in their home state during the lame-duck session before Democrats take control of the Senate on January 3.

"He's not from Texas," Cornyn told Reuters. "He has no trial experience, and the White House was trying to jam him down our throat without adequate vetting for a lifetime job."

A White House official in a statement said it expects all of Trump's judicial nominees to be confirmed by year's end.

Senators traditionally help choose nominees for vacancies on federal courts in their states. By Senate custom, they can effectively veto trial court nominees they oppose in their states by refusing to return a blue slip, a form used to signal support.

Trump nominated Gaiser, 37, to a seat on the US District Court for the Northern District of Texas after the election.

The former Ohio solicitor general previously clerked for conservative US Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito and currently heads the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel, a key unit that has frequently signed off on the legality of his administration's actions.

Cornyn, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee who lost a primary to a Trump-backed challenger, during Wednesday's hearing expressed support for Trump's decision to separately nominate Texas Supreme Court Justice James Sullivan to serve as a federal judge after he was defeated by a Democrat in the recent election.

But Cornyn has been pushing for the White House to pick someone else for the seat Gaiser was nominated to fill, recommending instead former federal prosecutor Steve Fahey of Texas.

"And the White House now seems to be showing some interest in that," Cornyn said in an interview.

Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas, who supports Gaiser, in a statement warned that the White House has indicated that it would be "impossible for a brand-new nominee to complete the FBI background check fast enough to be confirmed."

"If the Senate Judiciary Committee does not move Gaiser forward, the people of Texas will pay the price because it will effectively give the judicial seat to the Democrats, who will keep it vacant in perpetuity," Cruz said.

Two of Trump's other judicial nominees similarly ran into resistance from Republican senators in their home states after the midterm elections.

The White House on November 10 rescinded US District Judge Lee Rudofsky's nomination to the 8th US Circuit ​Court of Appeals and nominated Arkansas Supreme Court Justice J. Cody Hiland in his place following opposition from Arkansas' Republican senator. Hiland appeared at Wednesday's hearing with six other nominees.

data.title: Fed policymakers focused on inflation risks in October, with some seeing need for bigger rate hike
data.description:
Key points:
  • Fed held policy rate in 3.75%-4.00% range at October meeting
  • Inflation has been accelerating well beyond Fed's 2% target
  • A 'couple' of policymakers said half-percentage-point rate hike might be needed

By Howard Schneider

Federal Reserve officials saw a growing risk last month that they might need to intensify their efforts to control inflation, even as they agreed to keep interest rates steady for the moment, the minutes of their October 27-28 meeting showed on Wednesday.

"Almost all" policymakers agreed that further rate hikes would be needed if the economy evolved as they expected, the minutes said, while a few said inflation could prove more persistent and require "a shift to a more restrictive policy stance" than currently expected.

"A couple" of them went further and argued that the Fed might have to resort to a half-percentage-point increase "if incoming inflation data were unfavorable," a benchmark met in recent releases that showed prices rising faster than anticipated.

Among those who supported keeping the policy rate steady in the 3.75%-4.00% range in October, "a few ... indicated that they viewed the decision as a close call," and joined a larger group in urging that the Fed be clear that "the decision to maintain the target range did not reflect a weakening" of the commitment to hit the US central bank's 2% inflation target.

At the end of the two-day session, only Fed Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack dissented in favor of lifting the policy rate by a quarter of a percentage point.

But the debate highlighted a growing sense at the Fed that inflation will not ease enough on its own for the target to be reached quickly enough. Among those supporting a rate-hike pause, the hope is that coming information will make clearer whether inflation can fall without tighter policy.

Prices have been increasing at more than a 3% annual rate, and there has been little improvement in recent months.

Last month's meeting also set the stage for a potentially intense debate at the December 8-9 session over the need for a larger rate hike, or at least tougher language about the extent and pace of rate hikes to come, an argument laid out by Fed Governor Christopher Waller in comments to CNBC on Wednesday.

The Trump administration has argued that elevated inflation is just temporary and the Fed should ignore it.

Inflation has been stronger than expected since the Fed's last meeting, and investors anticipate that the central bank will deliver a quarter-percentage-point rate increase at its meeting next month.

The October meeting also saw the beginnings of a more detailed discussion about the impact of artificial intelligence, including discussion of the risks of over-investment in the technology as well as the possible benefits it could bring in the form of rising productivity.

data.title: Swiss Market Ends Moderately Lower
data.description:
BRUSSELS (dpa-AFX) - After opening flat and then moving slightly above the flat line till noon, the Switzerland market's benchmark SMI retreated and kept moving down till the end of the session on Wednesday.

Worries about inflation and interest rates, and falling commodity prices rendered the mood bearish.

The SMI ended the day with a loss of 89.92 points or 0.6% at 14,886.12, slightly off the day's low.

Julius Baer shed a little over 2%. Sandoz Group ended down 1.8%, while Helvetia Baloise Holding, Zurich Insurance, Novartis and UBS Group dropped 1.3%-1.6%.

Swiss Life Holding, Schindler Ps, Swiss Re, Swisscom, Geberit, Nestle, Partners Group and Kuehne + Nagel also closed weak.

Logitech International climbed nearly 3%. Richemont gained 1.45% and Sonovia avanced 1.05%. Alcon, Straumann Holding, Lonza Group, Holcim and VAT Group posted modest gains.

data.title: Spillover From Higher Energy Costs in Canada Has Been Central Bank's Main Concern — Market Talk
data.description:
1401 ET - Canada is seeing the spillover from higher energy costs spread, which was the central bank's main concern when it lifted its policy rate for the first time in more than three years, Bank of Canada Deputy Governor Toni Gravelle says. Speaking in Alberta, Gravelle says that as the risks to inflation shifted upward policymakers felt they didn't have as much scope to provide monetary policy accommodation. The BoC has a set of models that look higher up the supply chain when energy prices are higher, and found costs of imported goods and also outside of energy are also going up. Oil price shocks are usually transitory, but the longer they stay high the less likely it is business won't pass that along, Gravelle says. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

1355 ET - Massive investment in AI is supporting the dollar, Deutsche Bank analysts say in a report as they raise their forecast for the greenback. "The AI boom has been the big factor --it has pushed US real rates higher, attracted massive equity inflows, prompted renewed inflation pressure and a hawkish Fed," they say. On balance, "the 'AI dollar' is alive and well." Deutsche Bank now expects dollar strength into 1H of 2027 with "modest weakness" in 2H. A potential headwind: a downgrade to capex expectations would undermine the dollar strength. The WSJ Dollar Index rises 0.2%. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1306 ET - There's a perfect storm of three factors hitting bitcoin all at once, analysts from Yield Basis say in a research note. For one, investors now expect the Fed to raise interest rates in December, making yieldless assets more expensive to hold, they say. Secondly, there is a selloff in AI stocks that is forcing funds to decrease their risks, the analysts say. And lastly, bitcoin fell below its 200-day average, causing more than $2 billion of long positions to be forcibly closed out over the weekend, they say. On top of all that, there are concerns that AI and quantum computing could break encryption, which is tough for crypto's underdeveloped defenses, the analysts say. Bitcoin is down 1.7% at $62,830. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1207 ET - Non-U.S. buyers seem to be a key driver of recent dollar strength, Deutsche Bank's George Saravelos writes as the DXY dollar gauge hovers around a 19-month high, at 103.83. Hawkish Fedspeak also supports the currency, but Saravelos suspects it isn't enough. A Deutsche Bank tracker following more than 100 foreign-domiciled ETFs shows "extremely large dip-buying of US stocks from foreigners over the last two weeks, the largest buying spree so far this year," Saravelos says. He is skeptical that the trend will last "if market turmoil persists." (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1146 ET - Higher-taxpayers miss an opportunity in municipal bonds as they have a tendency to sell when yields rise, says Andrew Clinton of munis-focused Clinton Asset Management. Since bond prices fall when yields rise, Clinton says investors should add to their munis position when rates move upward. "There's a tendency for investors in fixed income, and munis specifically, to buy high and sell low," he says. "When the price falls, or the asset is on sale, you should be adding to it, not selling it." Clinton says demand remains high enough to absorb increasing munis supply, but it is concentrated on one- to 10-year maturities, leaving longer-dated bonds to yield beefy returns. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.com; @ptrevisani)

1136 ET - A wave of state-level tax hikes targeting high earners boosts the appeal of tax-exempt municipal bonds, says Andrew Clinton of Clinton Asset Management. He points to recent ballot measures alongside potential federal tax increases following midterm shifts and the possible expiration of current tax cuts. Clinton says investors can secure beefy returns while avoiding the volatility of equities. "Munis are one of the few asset classes where the actual value of the tax-free cash flow actually goes up should tax rates also increase," he says. (paulo.trevisani@wsj.co; @ptrevisani)

1105 ET - October home sales fell to their lowest level since 2010, in the pit of the Great Recession, Bankrate analyst Jeff Ostrowski says in a note. He points out how bizarre the current housing dynamic is compared to other parts of the economy. "If I were to say, 'Imagine a time when home prices are at record highs, the stock market has soared and the job market is near full employment,' you'd probably say, 'Wow - I bet Realtors are killing it!,'" he says. But prospective homebuyers are clearly turned off by high home prices and mortgage rates above 7%, Ostrowski says. That presents an opportunity for buyers to find a deal, so long as they can stomach the rates, he says. (dean.seal@wsj.com)

1045 ET - The U.K. inflation data released on Wednesday and the jobs data released on Tuesday fail to show evidence of second-order inflation effect, reducing the prospects of the Bank of England raising rates at the Dec. 17, meeting, J.P. Morgan's Allan Monks says in a note. U.K. annual core inflation remained unchanged in October at 2.8%, below the BOE forecast of 2.9% and annual services inflation stood at 3.7%, undershooting the BOE forecast of 3.9%. The data doesn't provide a compelling reason for the BOE to raise rates rapidly, after the rate rise delivered in November, Monks says. J.P. Morgan expects a BOE rate rise in February and a potential further rate increase in the second quarter of 2027. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

1003 ET - Canadian home prices ticked higher for a third month in the last four in October, based on the latest Teranet-National Bank data. Prices rose 0.2% nationally for the month, effectively extending a period of broadly stable prices since May following a period of contraction that began in December last year. National Bank economist Daren King says the latest modest gain remains fragile, tough, with only four of the home price index's 11 markets posting increases during the month. The advance was largely supported by a 5.8% jump in Halifax, Nova Scotia. King says the plateau reached nationally masks significant disparities between markets, and the composite home price index remains 7.9% below its April 2022 peak. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0958 ET - Leaked documents about Deutsche Bank's operations could damage the bank's reputation but appear less likely to damage its financial position, CreditSights' Simon Adamson says in a note. Most of the revelations are based on historic events and they are already known, Adamson says. "Despite the embarrassing headlines, the consequences for Deutsche Bank look fairly limited at this stage." CreditSights maintains a "market perform" view on Deutsche Bank's additional tier 1 (AT 1) bonds, and an "outperform" view on the bank's non-preferred senior bonds. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0930 ET - Higher Swiss inflation and a weaker euro could leave the Swiss franc stronger than expected, Raiffeisen Research's Amadea Zaborszky-Hiess says in a note. Annual inflation rose to 1.5% in October from 1.0% in September, increasing the likelihood of the Swiss National Bank raising interest rates, she says. "While second-round effects remain limited for now, persistently high oil prices pose a risk of broader inflationary pressures." Raiffeisen's franc forecast was already at risk of being revised amid euro weakness on French fiscal concerns, and stronger inflationary pressures have amplified those risks, she says. For now, Raiffeisen maintains a forecast of the euro rising to 0.94 francs by year-end from 0.9246 currently before falling in the quarters ahead. (renae.dyer@wsj.com)

0912 ET - The euro is the weakest among the G-10 currencies, analysts at Bannockburn Capital Markets say in a note. Renewed pressure on eurozone peripheral and French bonds are helping to drag the euro lower, they say. The euro falls 0.3% to $1.0968 after reaching a 19-month low of $1.0952 earlier, according to LSEG. The 10-year German Bund yield falls 0.6 basis points to 3.382%, the 10-year French OAT yield is down 4 basis points at 4.863% and the 10-year Italian BTP yield declines 0.9 basis points to 4.428%, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)
